reason: FAQ answers 'No' to using CloudHSM without a VPC and says it must be provisioned inside an Amazon VPC to protect and isolate the cluster from other customers.

FAQ says the rotation strategy depends on the application type, shows the customer rotating by creating a new key, and for envelope encryption says you will need to create a rotation tool and process if you have none.
FAQ lists PKCS#11, Java JCE, OpenSSL Dynamic Engine and Microsoft KSP/CNG as standard APIs a custom application can use.
Context says AWS backs up daily and you are solely responsible for key durability in the 24-hour period between backups; quote strongly recommends syncing keys to at least two HSMs in two AZs.
Quote states physical and logical tamper detection and response trigger key deletion (zeroization) of the hardware.
Quote names Oracle Database 19c, Apache and Nginx for SSL offload, and configuring Windows Server as a CA as integrated and tested.
Three quotes state HA from HSMs in different AZs, the recommended minimum of two HSMs per cluster in different AZs of a Region, and automatic load balancing with more than one HSM.

Quotes support HSM users instead of IAM users or policies inside the cluster and that IAM users can create HSMs through the AWS API, but nothing says IAM controls ONLY HSM creation; the word 'only' goes beyond the quote.

Dates (end of support March 31st 2026, no new hsm1 clusters from April 2025, auto-migration from January 2026) are supported, but no quote ties hsm1.medium to FIPS 140-2 Level 3; the FAQ quote is about CloudHSM in general.
FAQ says hsm2m.medium instances are single-tenant and FIPS 140-3 Level 3 certified, with a non-FIPS mode option.
Quotes state CloudTrail captures all CloudHSM API calls, does not include HSM device or access logs, and CloudHSM sends HSM audit logs to CloudWatch Logs on your behalf.
System quotas row gives 3,300 (hsm1.medium) and 16,666 total with asymmetric max 3,333 (hsm2m.medium) per cluster; the page states the System Quotas table is not adjustable.
System quotas row gives 250 users per cluster for hsm1.medium and 1,024 for hsm2m.medium.
Quote states the E2E-encrypted data plane is not visible to AWS, you control your own user management, and you have more responsibility than with a managed service.

Numbers are right (the hsm2m.medium table at line 30 has the same RSA row), but the matched context is the hsm1.medium table with no heading scoping it to hsm2m, and qualifier default_or_max 'max' is not stated; the page gives approximate benchmark figures, not maximums.
Claim text is supported (no upfront costs, hourly fee per HSM until terminated), but the qualifier condition (fee varies by Region; data transfer charged separately) is not in this fact's quote.
FAQ quotes state hourly fee per hour or partial hour an HSM is provisioned, no billing for a cluster without HSMs or for backup storage, and data transfer charged separately.
Service quotas row 'Clusters | 4 | Yes' under 'Default Quota | Adjustable?'; the page intro says the quotas apply per AWS Region and AWS account.
Service quotas row 'HSMs per cluster | 28 | No' gives 28 and not adjustable.
Service quotas row 'HSMs | 6 | Yes'; the page intro says the quotas apply per AWS Region and AWS account.
FAQ answers 'Not directly' and says to use AWS KMS with Custom Key Store to secure RDS data with keys generated and stored in the CloudHSM cluster.
FAQ states a single-HSM cluster can lose keys created since the last daily backup, and clusters with two or more HSMs, ideally in separate AZs, will not lose keys if one HSM fails.
FAQ states single-tenant access to the HSM; hardware may be shared but the HSM is accessible only to you.
Quote states the quotas in the System Quotas table are not adjustable; the table holds the per-cluster keys, users and client connection quotas.
Use-cases page names SSL/TLS offload for web servers, storing the TDE master encryption key, and storing issuing CA private keys for signing.
Quotes describe admin and CU duties, but only 'In CloudHSM CLI' (page 'HSM user types for CloudHSM CLI'); the claim drops that scope, and the earlier CMU tool uses different user types.
Quotes state automatic resynchronization applies only to keys, users and policies are not resynchronized, and CloudHSM CLI does best-effort sync that may need manual resolution.
KMS FAQ comparison states a validated single-tenant HSM cluster in your VPC, exclusive control via authentication independent from AWS, and PKCS#11, Java JCE or Microsoft CNG interfaces.
Quote defines an HSM as a device that processes cryptographic operations and securely stores keys; context says CloudHSM gives you HSMs in the AWS Cloud.
Quote states an account-principal statement gives no IAM principal permission and lets the account use IAM policies to delegate the permissions.
Quotes say asymmetric keys are a good choice for encryption outside AWS by users who cannot call KMS, and to use a symmetric encryption key for data stored or managed in an AWS service.
Quotes state the private key is created in KMS and never leaves it unencrypted, and the public key can be downloaded and used outside KMS.
Quotes give the aws/<service-name> alias format (example aws/redshift) and state the aws/ prefix is reserved and cannot be used to create an alias.
Quotes list view keys, view policies and audit in CloudTrail as allowed, and no property changes, rotation, policy changes, deletion scheduling or direct cryptographic use.
Quote defines AWS managed keys as KMS keys in your account created, managed and used on your behalf by an integrated AWS service.

Claim text is supported (legacy type, not created for new services as of 2021, services use AWS owned keys by default), but the qualifier condition 'existing AWS managed keys keep working' is not stated in the quote.
Quotes state automatic yearly rotation (about 365 days), that you cannot enable or disable it, and the May 2022 change from every three years (about 1,095 days).
Quotes state AWS owned keys are a good choice unless you must audit or control the key, are free of charge, do not count against KMS quotas, and need no key policy maintenance.
Quotes state AWS owned keys are owned and managed by a service for use in multiple accounts, are not in your account, and can protect resources in your account.
Prescriptive guidance quote states transparent encryption at rest is the standard security posture across the service portfolio, without requiring explicit configuration.
